opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting problem, and I'd say it's less about one big trick and more about a bunch of things that all have to work together.

The first challenge is just sequence length. Audio tokens add up very quickly, so even with a good codec, an hour of speech is a lot of tokens. You can't naively generate that in one context window and expect it to stay coherent. So you have to think about how you compress the audio representation, and how you structure generation so the model works on manageable chunks while still knowing what came before.

The second, and honestly the harder one, is consistency. For a short clip, people forgive a lot. Over an hour, you notice immediately if the voice drifts, if the speaker's timbre changes slightly, if the pacing gets weird, or if the energy flattens out. So you need some kind of persistent conditioning: a speaker representation that stays anchored, plus a summary of the context, so minute fifty sounds like the same person as minute one.

Then there's the prosody side. Long-form content like audiobooks or podcasts isn't just reading sentences one after another. There's structure: paragraphs, chapters, emphasis, pauses, and the speaker reacting to what they said earlier. A model that only sees the current sentence will sound fine locally but kind of monotone globally. So you want the model to have access to the broader text, ideally the whole document or a good representation of it, so it can plan delivery the way a human narrator would.

And of course evaluation is tricky. Most TTS metrics are designed for short utterances. For hour-long audio, you really need people to listen to long stretches, and you want automatic checks for drift and for errors like skipped or repeated words, because those compound over time.

So the way I think about it is: get the representation efficient enough, keep the conditioning stable, give the model enough global context to plan, and build evaluation that actually reflects long-form listening. None of these is completely solved, but they're very tractable, and I think we'll see a lot of progress there quite soon.

r001.rationale: The response says audio tokens accumulate quickly and that an hour cannot be generated naively in one context window; it does not say a low audio token rate makes this feasible.

r002.rationale: It discusses chunking, persistent conditioning, and broader context, but does not connect these methods to techniques used for long-context text modeling.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify autoregressive flow matching or distinguish it from text-token prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that we didn't design the first version for that. When we built the TTS model, the target was really the conversational regime: short utterances, low latency, something you can put behind an agent and have it respond in a few hundred milliseconds. Hour-long audio is a very different problem, and I'd say it's different along three axes.

The first is just the sequence length. Audio tokens are expensive. Even with a good neural codec running at a low frame rate, an hour of speech is on the order of hundreds of thousands of tokens, and if you try to do that in a single autoregressive pass with full attention, you're paying a quadratic cost and you're also asking the model to hold a context it was never trained on. So the naive approach, which is "just extend the context window," doesn't really work. What we do instead is chunk. You generate segment by segment, and the question becomes: what do you carry across the boundary? And the answer is not the raw audio history, it's a compressed state. You condition each new segment on a speaker embedding, on a short acoustic prefix from the previous segment so the prosody doesn't jump, and on the text context around the boundary so the model knows where it is in the sentence. That gives you something that scales linearly and that you can stream.

The second axis is consistency, and I think this is the one people underestimate. If you generate ten seconds of speech, the voice sounds fine. If you generate sixty minutes, you start to see drift. The pitch creeps up, the speaking rate changes, the model falls into a kind of attractor where everything becomes monotone, or the opposite, it starts hallucinating emphasis in weird places. This is the same phenomenon you see in long text generation where the model slowly loses the plot, except in audio it's very audible to a human. So you need an explicit anchor. The speaker representation has to be a fixed conditioning signal that the model is strongly tied to, not something it infers from the recent context, otherwise the error compounds. And we found that training with longer segments, even if you can't train on an hour, matters a lot. If the model has only ever seen five-second clips, it has never learned what "the same voice twenty seconds later" looks like.

The third axis is the one that's less about the audio model and more about the text. For an hour of content, the interesting part is not the acoustics, it's the structure. Pauses between paragraphs, how you handle a quote versus narration, where you breathe, how the energy changes across a long passage. A short-form TTS model has no notion of that because it never sees documents, it sees sentences. So you end up wanting the model to take as input something richer than plain text, something more like a script with structure, and that's where having a strong text model in the same stack helps. You can have the LLM do the planning, decide the pacing and the emphasis, and the TTS model execute it. I think of it a bit like the separation between a director and an actor. The acoustic model is a very good actor, but it doesn't need to understand the whole book.

And then there's the practical side, which is evaluation. For short utterances, you can use MOS scores, you can do pairwise comparisons, people listen to a clip. Nobody is going to listen to an hour of generated audio and tell you whether it was good. So you need proxy metrics that capture drift, things like speaker similarity measured at the beginning versus the end, word error rate from a transcription pass across the whole thing, prosody statistics over time. Those are imperfect, but they're what let you iterate.

So I'd say it's less about a bigger model and more about the system around it. Chunked generation with a compressed state, a strong fixed speaker anchor, training on longer segments than you think you need, and letting the text model handle the long-range structure. That's the direction I find most convincing.

r001.rationale: The response says an hour requires hundreds of thousands of audio tokens and that simply extending the context window does not work; it proposes chunking instead.

r002.rationale: It compares long-audio drift to long-text generation, but does not say that the methods for extending speech generation are similar to long-context text modeling.

r003.rationale: It does not identify autoregressive flow matching as the modeling difference; it discusses autoregressive generation and codec tokens without that distinction.

astra-6.text:
I would separate two things: generating an hour of speech from a script, and having the model decide what to say for an hour. For the first, you don’t necessarily need to generate everything in one pass. You could generate segments, conditioning each segment on enough of the previous audio to keep the voice and prosody consistent. The challenge is making those transitions feel natural, so it doesn’t sound like the speaker starts over every few sentences.

For the second, you also need coherence at the level of the content. That becomes a planning problem as well as an audio generation problem. I would probably start with a system that plans the content and then generates the speech incrementally. But I wouldn’t assume that a model that sounds good for thirty seconds will automatically sound good for an hour. You have to evaluate the consistency over that longer duration.

r001.rationale: The response discusses segmented generation and consistency, but does not mention a low audio token rate or feasibility within a long context window.

r002.rationale: It proposes incremental generation and content planning, but does not connect the approach to techniques used for long-context text modeling.

r003.rationale: It does not identify autoregressive flow matching or distinguish it from text-token prediction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main challenge is maintaining consistency over that duration. Generating an hour of audio is one thing, but keeping the same voice, the same style, and natural prosody throughout is another.

You probably don’t want to generate the whole thing in a single pass. You can split the text into segments, but then you need to carry enough context between them so that each segment doesn’t sound like a fresh recording. And you need some understanding of the longer structure—where to pause, where to change emphasis, how the tone should evolve.

So I would think about it as a hierarchical problem: plan at the level of the whole document, then generate locally while preserving continuity. Streaming also matters, because you want people to start listening without waiting for the entire hour to be generated.
